acceptedAnswer.text: The heat index is the 'feels like' temperature that combines air temperature and relative humidity. High humidity prevents sweat from evaporating, making it feel hotter. At 90°F with 70% humidity, the heat index is 106°F.
The NWS uses the Rothfusz regression equation, a polynomial formula involving temperature (°F) and relative humidity (%). The formula includes 9 terms and adjustment factors for extreme conditions.

80-90°F: Caution (fatigue possible). 90-103°F: Extreme Caution (heat cramps/exhaustion possible). 103-124°F: Danger (heat cramps/exhaustion likely, heatstroke possible). 125°F+: Extreme Danger (heatstroke highly likely).

mainEntity.name: What is the highest heat index ever recorded?

acceptedAnswer.text: The highest heat index values exceeding 170°F have been calculated in the Middle East. Dhahran, Saudi Arabia recorded a dew point of 95°F in 2003, producing an extreme heat index. In the US, heat indices above 130°F have occurred in the desert Southwest.

mainEntity.name: Why does humidity make it feel hotter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your body cools itself through sweat evaporation. When humidity is high, sweat cannot evaporate efficiently, so your body cannot cool down. This makes the effective temperature feel much higher than the actual air temperature.

mainEntity.name: Is heat index calculated in the shade or sun?

acceptedAnswer.text: The heat index is calculated for shady conditions with light wind. Full sunshine can increase the heat index by up to 15°F. Physical activity also increases the danger level regardless of the calculated heat index.

howItWorks.intro: The NWS Rothfusz regression is a nine-term polynomial, not a simple lookup table — it was built by regressing Steadman's biometeorological heat-stress model against a grid of temperature and humidity combinations for an adult walking in the shade. It's the same equation federal and state occupational heat-safety guidance points to whenever it references "heat index," which is why this calculator runs the full polynomial rather than a simplified chart or a linear approximation between reference points.

rules.name: Heat Index (NWS Rothfusz Regression)
rules.explanation: T is dry-bulb air temperature in °F and R is relative humidity as a whole-number percentage. Below 13% RH with T between 80-112°F, a low-humidity correction term is subtracted; above 85% RH with T between 80-87°F, a high-humidity correction term is added. Below 80°F, the NWS instead uses a simpler averaging formula, since humidity has little effect on perceived temperature in that range.

howItWorks.outro: Keep in mind the regression models a person walking in the shade at a light pace — it doesn't account for radiant heat coming off asphalt, metal roofing, or reflective concrete, and it doesn't account for moderate-to-heavy physical exertion or PPE that traps body heat and blocks sweat evaporation. Roofers, road crews, and framers routinely face effective heat loads well above what the calculator shows once you add a hard hat, a dark shirt, direct sun, and hours of sustained work — treat this output as your starting point for the day, not the ceiling for how hot the job will feel by early afternoon.

faqHTML:
Frequently Asked Questions

What is the heat index?

The heat index combines air temperature and relative humidity to determine what the temperature "feels like" to the human body. High humidity reduces the body's ability to cool through sweat evaporation.

How is heat index calculated?

The NWS uses the Rothfusz regression equation, a 9-term polynomial formula using temperature and humidity, with adjustment factors applied at extremes. It is valid for temperatures at or above 80°F.

What heat index is dangerous?

Caution at 80-90°F (fatigue possible). Extreme Caution at 90-103°F (heat cramps/exhaustion possible). Danger at 103-124°F (heat exhaustion likely). Extreme Danger above 125°F (heatstroke imminent).

What is the highest heat index ever recorded?

Heat indices exceeding 170°F have been calculated in the Persian Gulf region. In the US, values above 130°F have occurred in the desert Southwest during extreme heat events.

Why does humidity make it feel hotter?

Your body cools by sweating. When humidity is high, sweat cannot evaporate efficiently, trapping heat. At 90°F with 40% humidity the heat index is 88°F, but at 90% humidity it jumps to 109°F.

Is heat index calculated in the shade or sun?

The official heat index assumes shade with light wind. Direct sun can add up to 15°F to the perceived temperature. Physical activity further increases heat stress risk beyond what the index shows.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator runs the full nine-term Rothfusz polynomial in your browser using your entered temperature and humidity — the same regression behind the National Weather Service's official heat index charts and the one many state and federal occupational heat-safety standards reference directly.
steps: Enter the dry-bulb air temperature (°F) from a job-site thermometer, weather station, or forecast, plus the relative humidity as a percentage
The calculator evaluates the full Rothfusz polynomial rather than interpolating a printed chart, so you get the same precision behind official NWS heat advisories
If your inputs fall in an edge case — very low humidity at high temperature, or very high humidity at moderate temperature — the NWS correction terms are applied automatically
The result returns both the feels-like heat index and its NWS danger band, so you can match it against a work-rest or hydration policy
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This is an informational planning tool, not a certified heat-stress monitor and not medical guidance. It calculates shaded-air heat index only — it does not measure wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), account for direct sun, radiant heat from work surfaces, physical exertion, or an individual's hydration and acclimatization status, all of which can push real heat stress well above the number shown. For workplace heat-illness prevention programs, follow your employer's written heat-safety plan and applicable OSHA or state standards, and treat symptoms of heat exhaustion or heatstroke as a medical emergency.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this when the day's plan involves sustained outdoor exertion in the heat, not just a comfort check before a walk.
scenarios: Briefing a construction, roofing, or road crew before a shift to decide whether today calls for standard or heat-modified work-rest cycles
Setting hydration and shade-break frequency for agricultural, landscaping, or delivery workers under NIOSH-style guidance
Checking conditions in non-climate-controlled indoor spaces — warehouses, kitchens, manufacturing floors — where a temperature and humidity reading is available but air conditioning isn't
Logging heat index alongside other conditions in a safety incident report or daily job-site log
Deciding whether a heat advisory or excessive-heat warning actually changes today's outdoor work plan, versus a forecast headline that sounds worse than the on-site numbers

By entering your air temperature, relative humidity, you get instant results including heat index, danger level, health risks. No formulas to memorize, no spreadsheets to build — just enter your numbers and get the answer in seconds. Whether you're a beginner or experienced professional, this calculator saves you time and eliminates guesswork.
